uvapages.content: h1: Uva Pages 2.0 — The story editor the newsroom runs on its own Design and programming In use at Estadão since 2023 Each visual story needed a developer to put the page together, so the graphics desk waited. I designed and programmed Uva Pages 2.0, fully optimized to work directly from a Google Docs document. The story is written there, a custom menu inserts images, charts, quizzes, and scrollytelling, and the page is built from components that already exist. Since 2023, every story published by Estadão’s multimedia team has been made with it. {fluxo} titulo: How Uva Pages builds a story titulo_esquerda: The newsroom esquerda_1: Google Docs | The reporter or designer writes the story there esquerda_2: Markup | A custom menu inserts images, charts, and scrollytelling esquerda_3: page.json | ArchieML turns the document into structured data titulo_direita: The code direita_1: Svelte components | One for each kind of block direita_2: bundle.js | Compiled once, shared by every story fim_1: Render fim_2: The published page {} The deck below presents the tool, in Spanish. pdf: UvaPages.pdf

{imagem} nome: fabio-sales-about.jpg alt: Portrait of Fabio Sales tamanho: PP classes: var(--shadow-2) borda: 50% {} h1: I design clarity inside complex systems For three decades, I have worked across visual design, product, technology, and business — leading multidisciplinary teams, creating systems, and staying close to the craft. My career did not move from design to technology. It expanded from designing information to designing the systems, interactions, and software through which people experience it. {faixa} pasta: faixa-about tempo: 100 imagem_1: atbl-giro.jpg | Stock turnover and reordering in the ATBL products app imagem_2: estadao-tsunami-2011.jpg | Earthquake and tsunami in Japan, Estadão, March 12, 2011 imagem_3: atbl-vale.jpg | A hose assembly order in the ATBL workshop app imagem_4: estadao-arena-2012.jpg | Arena Corinthians infographic, Estadão, December 2, 2012 imagem_5: estadao-tetra-2014.jpg | Sports cover on the World Cup final, Estadão, July 14, 2014 imagem_6: correio-2002.jpg | “Enfim, lá!”, Correio Braziliense, 2002 imagem_7: atbl-movimentacao.jpg | Stock movements in the ATBL products app {} h3: Craft is where it started Visual journalism taught me to make unfamiliar, dense information understandable under real constraints and real deadlines. At Estadão, Diário de Notícias, Correio Braziliense, and through international consulting, I worked across typography, information architecture, data visualization, art direction, interaction, and storytelling — while leading teams responsible for products used by large audiences. That work earned hundreds of national and international distinctions for the teams I led; the timeline on the home page plots only the ones I could confirm in public records. h3: Leadership means building the conditions for good work I believe a design leader has two responsibilities at the same time: raise the quality bar and build an environment in which teams can reach it repeatedly. h3: Technology extended the design surface Since 2010, I have increasingly worked with software as part of the design process. Today I build with JavaScript, Svelte, React, Python, SQL, APIs, ERP integrations, and AI-assisted workflows. It lets me prototype ideas and take product decisions all the way to production. h3: Today At ATBL I lead the digital transformation and help run the company: people management, the reorganization of the sales department around a new team of salespeople, finance, and stock. The problems are very different from a newsroom, but the design challenge is familiar: complex rules, fragmented information, and users who should not have to understand the infrastructure underneath. {divisor} {capitulos} titulo: Selected career chapters capitulo_1: ATBL | 2025–Present | Transformation and Innovation leadership, and company administration. Product strategy, digital operations, ERP integration, AI workflows, and hands-on product development. imagem_1: capitulos/atbl-telas.png legenda_1: Delivery routes, the workshop panel, and stock put-away in the ATBL apps. capitulo_2: Independent | 2023–2025 | Product, technology, and business-process consulting; full-stack development and automation. capitulo_3: Estadão | 2005–2023 | Executive Art Editor. Front pages built on one strong image and one headline. In 2002 the paper won 36 Society for News Design awards, more than in any other year of its history, and was the most awarded Latin American newspaper in the competition. imagem_5: capitulos/correio-capa-2001.jpg legenda_5: “Os selvagens venceram”, front page of December 9, 2001. papel_5: sim capitulo_6: O Dia and O Globo | 1997–2000 | Designer, later deputy art editor. blue_case.content: {imagem} nome: blue/tablet.png tamanho: M alt: The Blue prototype on a tablet, with the section bar across the top and a story below tags: Product Design, UX/UI, Interaction Design {} h1: Blue — Designing for a New Interaction Model Interface design and prototype 2010 Blue was created in 2010, when the tablet was still an emerging consumer platform. Rather than treat the device as a smaller desktop, the project asked: what changes when people navigate information primarily with their hands? h3: The context Financial news is continuous, dense, and time-sensitive. A touch device introduced different constraints from desktop: direct manipulation, changing orientation, less visible navigation chrome, and a stronger relationship between gesture and spatial movement. h3: The interaction hypothesis We explored gesture-based navigation and card-like structures for moving through the news stream. The goal was to create a spatial model people could understand through touch rather than reproduce the desktop interface. h3: Designing before the pattern library existed Today cards, swipes, touch targets, and responsive information blocks are ordinary vocabulary. At the time those conventions were still being negotiated. Blue was R&D as much as interface design: prototype, understand the medium, and establish useful patterns rather than wait for mature conventions to copy. h3: Why it still matters The visual language belongs to 2010. The product question does not: understand the capabilities and constraints of the platform, then design behavior around people rather than around the previous technology. ← Back to selected work

estadao.content:
h1: Estadão — Designing a System at Scale Executive Art Editor, lead of the redesign Over 18 years at the company, at times I coordinated about 75 people across these roles: designers, photographers, infographic artists, illustrators, and data journalists 2021, in an 18-year tenure {antesDepois} antes: estadao/formato-standard.jpg depois: estadao/formato-berliner.jpg rotulo_antes: Standard, 2018 rotulo_depois: Berliner, 2021 alt: Two Estadão front pages at the same scale: the standard format of 2018 and the smaller Berliner format of 2021 legenda: Front pages of January 25, 2018 and October 26, 2021, at the same scale. Drag to compare: the new page is 13 centimetres shorter and one column narrower. tamanho: P {} A newspaper redesign can look like a graphic-design exercise. The real challenge was systemic: evolve a daily information product while balancing readers, editorial priorities, industrial production, advertising, digital workflows, and business performance. {numeros} numero_1: 18 | Years at the paper, from 2005 to 2023 numero_2: R$7 million | Estimated EBITDA increase in 2022, according to the business case numero_3: 3 | Fronts the redesign had to serve at once: editorial, production, and advertising {} h3: A high-frequency interface before we called it product design Every day the content changes completely. The interface cannot. Readers need to recognize hierarchy and scan dense information in seconds; editors need flexibility without rebuilding the language every morning. Create enough consistency to make the product intuitive, and enough flexibility to keep it expressive. {imagem} nome: estadao/novo-estadao-capa.jpg tamanho: GG legenda: The special section that presented the new Estadão to readers, October 17, 2021. {} h3: The format was decided with readers I led the redesign across editorial, production, and advertising. The first thing to settle was the format. In the last of five surveys over eleven months, we sent three printed prototypes to 100 subscribers and interviewed them by video call. 89% preferred the Berliner format; all of them found it easier to hold, and 88% found it more comfortable to read. The new page kept practically the same column width, with larger type and more space between lines, and the launch edition walked readers through what was new. {imagem} nome: estadao/pesquisa-recorte.jpg tamanho: GG legenda: The research as the paper published it on October 17, 2021. {} A UX researcher on this process: “Quando o jornal vira notícia” (LinkedIn) ↗ h3: From pages to reusable decisions The page became 13 centimetres shorter and one column narrower. Typography, hierarchy, and the recurring modules were redrawn for the new grid, so editors build each page from known parts instead of starting from zero every morning. Explore the redesign and design system ↗
Explore interactive & multimedia UI components → {imagem} nome: estadao/anatomia.jpg tamanho: GG legenda: “A anatomia do novo Estadão”, October 17, 2021. The spread explained the new format, sections, and typography to readers. {} h3: Craft and business The redesign supported production optimization and a new advertising strategy; its business case estimated a R$7 million increase in EBITDA in 2022. Read the strategic business case (PDF) ↗
See the advertising strategy (PDF) ↗ The new format in print: front pages from its first weeks and prototype pages. {faixa} pasta: faixa-estadao tempo: 120 papel: sim imagem_1: capa-2021-10-24.jpg | Front page, October 24, 2021 imagem_2: prototipo-afundo-1.jpg | Prototype spread for the A Fundo section, 2021 imagem_3: prototipo-sextou.jpg | Prototype page for Sextou!, the weekend guide, 2021 imagem_4: capa-2021-10-26.jpg | Front page, October 26, 2021 imagem_5: prototipo-afundo-2.jpg | Prototype spread for the A Fundo section, 2021 imagem_6: prototipo-reportagem.jpg | Prototype spread for special reports, 2021 imagem_7: prototipo-alias.jpg | Prototype spread for Aliás, 2021 imagem_8: capa-2021-11-04.jpg | Front page, November 4, 2021 imagem_9: prototipo-bem-estar.jpg | Prototype cover for the Bem-estar supplement, 2021 imagem_10: capa-2021-11-09.jpg | Front page, November 9, 2021 {} ← Back to selected work

atbl.content: {celular} pasta: atbl entrada: login.jpg entrada_alt: Sign-in screen of the ATBL shipping app alt: A phone showing the ATBL sign-in screen, with three app screens sliding out beside it tela_1: exp-02.jpg | The day's orders tela_2: ofi-14.jpg | Hose assembly tela_3: prod-06.jpg | Stock put-away {} h1: ATBL — Turning Enterprise Complexity into a Usable Product Transformation and Innovation lead; product design and programming 2025–present A commercial transaction sits on top of specifications, inventory, customer pricing, taxes, approvals, ERP processes, documentation, and relationships. The design question was which complexity users need to see — and which complexity the system should absorb for them. h3: One decision, followed through: shipping Orders were checked on paper. Labels were typed in Word, printed, and cut out by hand. Signed delivery receipts went into paper folders, filed by month and year; when a customer asked for one, finding it could take hours. Put the whole path on the phone and let the order in the ERP be the only source. Items are scanned against it, labels print from it, and the driver photographs the signed receipt at the door. We estimate that dispatching goods now takes at least half the time it did. Every receipt sits in a digital archive, attached to its invoice, and when a customer asks for proof we send a link. Eight screens from the shipping, workshop, and stock apps, as they are used today. {telas} pasta: atbl imagem_1: exp-02.jpg chapeu_1: Shipping titulo_1: The day's orders on one screen texto_1: How many orders are waiting, checked, labelled, and out for delivery. The shipping team opens the day here. imagem_2: exp-03.jpg chapeu_2: Shipping titulo_2: Checking against the order texto_2: Each item is scanned against the order from the ERP. A difference shows up before the box is closed, not at the customer. imagem_3: exp-05.jpg chapeu_3: Shipping titulo_3: The route, stop by stop texto_3: Deliveries are grouped by driver, with distance, time on the road, and the order of the stops. imagem_4: exp-10.jpg chapeu_4: Shipping titulo_4: Proof of delivery, photographed texto_4: The driver photographs the signed receipt, and it goes back to the ERP attached to the invoice. imagem_5: ofi-01.jpg chapeu_5: Workshop titulo_5: What the hose workshop produced texto_5: Pieces assembled and inspected, approval rate, and assembly time, by day, week, or month. imagem_6: ofi-14.jpg chapeu_6: Workshop titulo_6: Assembly, measured texto_6: The assembler records each crimping measurement against the tolerance. The app times the job without anyone pressing a stopwatch. imagem_7: ofi-19.jpg chapeu_7: Workshop titulo_7: The certificate, straight from the assembly texto_7: The test certificate is generated from what was recorded during assembly and inspection, ready to print. imagem_8: prod-06.jpg chapeu_8: Stock titulo_8: Every product has an address texto_8: On arrival, each item is scanned to a shelf position. The location is written to the product record. {} h3: The system behind the experience {sistema} titulo_cima: What people see visivel_1: Customer | A technical need and a commercial context. visivel_2: Portal and apps | Catalogue, stock, price, documents, and order status, on one screen. visivel_3: Delivery | Tracking and proof of delivery come back to the same place. titulo_baixo: What the system absorbs oculto_1: Inventory | by location, live from the ERP oculto_2: Customer pricing | agreements and price tables oculto_3: Taxes | calculated per order oculto_4: Approvals | credit and commercial rules oculto_5: Billing | the approved order, without retyping oculto_6: Records | what the app wrote, and when nota: Show what a decision needs. Absorb the rest. {} h3: Designing for technical B2B More than 26,000 active products require structured images, dimensions, attributes, standards, and technical metadata before an interface can make them meaningfully searchable. I designed and built products integrated with Sankhya ERP, keeping product decisions grounded in real inventory, pricing, and operational rules. h3: From interface to operating model Digital channels handle first-level service, stock and price checks, and order tracking; technical salespeople remain focused on engineering solutions and strategic negotiations. The company recorded a 12.5% revenue increase alongside these operational changes; I treat that as business context, not as a claim that interface design alone caused growth. h3: What is running today {numeros} numero_1: 6,359 | Deliveries recorded since July 2024 numero_2: 97% | Of confirmed deliveries have the proof of delivery attached numero_3: 9,269 | Hoses completed in the workshop since February 2025 numero_4: 99.9% | Of inspected hoses with a satisfactory result numero_5: 26,484 | Active products in the catalogue numero_6: 84% | Of the products sold online have a photo nota: Company records, as of October 13, 2026. {} The apps share one design system and the same foundations, and they read from and write to the ERP. ← Back to selected work

newsletters.content: {imagem} nome: newsletters/saiba-agora.jpg tamanho: P {} h1: Personalized Newsletters — Testing Relevance at Scale Lead of the Estadão team Editorial, commercial, digital strategy, reader revenue, and technology, with the startups Beluga and Itera 2020 A daily newsletter gives every reader the same editorial selection. This experiment asked whether recommendations based on reading behavior could make that selection more relevant — and whether the evidence would justify changing the product. h3: My contribution In 2020 I led the Estadão team behind the InovaBra newsletter experiment and represented the newspaper with Beluga and Itera, the two startups Bradesco had selected for the program. The team brought together colleagues from editorial, commercial, digital strategy, reader revenue, and technology, and put editorial judgment, recommendation systems, and audience measurement into the same product discussion. h3: An experiment inside an existing habit The test used Saiba Agora, an established subscriber briefing. Beluga and Itera each created five audience clusters using browsing history and two months of news coverage. Each partner recommended four stories per cluster. From December 10 to 16, 2020, the team sent eleven newsletter versions: five for each partner and one editorial control. Keeping the existing newsletter as a reference made it possible to compare personalization with the experience readers already knew. {numeros} numero_1: 11 | Newsletter versions sent: five for each partner and one editorial control numero_2: 10 | Audience clusters, five built by each partner numero_3: 4 | Stories recommended to each cluster numero_4: 7 | Days of testing, December 10 to 16 {} h3: Relevance needed more than a click The evaluation combined click-through rates on recommended stories, bounce rate, and reading time with a qualitative review of the editorial selections. Audience groups behaved differently, and the largest clusters strongly influenced the averages. {imagem} nome: newsletters/resultados.jpg tamanho: G {} h3: What the results actually showed Click-through results were close across Beluga, Itera, and Estadão. Some smaller clusters performed better, but the short test did not establish a clear overall uplift. Both partners showed lower bounce rates; reading time was higher for the existing Estadão selection. The useful signal was more specific: Beluga’s audience groups were more distinct, and its daily recommendations showed stronger affinity with those groups. Delivery processes and clarity of collaboration also mattered when assessing the next step. h3: The decision was another test The report recommended a further 30-day round with Beluga, ten refined clusters, and better automated measurement. That was a proposed next phase, not evidence of a completed rollout or a proven long-term gain. ← Back to selected work
